title: The Two Versions of a Meal Voucher
summary: Design a small pilot that measures access as well as completed transactions.

documents.title: Centre memo after the pilot
documents.text:
We offered the same lunch voucher in two forms during last month's pilot. Eighty digital codes were issued by email and sixty paper cards were handed out at community sessions. The digital system recorded forty-eight meals, while the signed paper list recorded thirty-six. Those numbers describe completed uses. They do not show whether someone tried to use a voucher and left without a meal.

At two cafés, the code scanner was beside the main till. At the other two, a member of staff had to fetch it from a drawer. Paper vouchers were signed by staff in all four cafés. The manager at Hill Café reported that the paper list took longer to check at closing, particularly when the same first name appeared twice.

The budgets for the formats were similar. Before choosing a format, we should consider what happens if visitors receive a voucher late or leave a phone at home. The weekend café also wants to know whether it can handle two kinds of record when several people arrive together.

documents.title: A coordinator's comparison sheet
documents.text:
The forms were offered through different routes. Visitors requesting email updates received digital codes. People at sessions could choose a paper card without giving an email address. We therefore cannot explain a difference between the groups simply by pointing to the format. Their usual ways of contacting the centre may also differ.

For a second pilot, we could give people a choice at two sessions and record which format they select. Staff would make one short mark if a transaction had to be restarted. The mark shows that something interrupted the process. It does not need a customer's name. Staff could select one reason from a small list after the customer leaves.

A person whose digital voucher will not load can show the printed booking reference. Staff can record a completed use on a separate sheet and verify it at closing. This fallback is for an unavailable code. It does not permit another meal when the same voucher has been used.

recordings.title: At the weekend till
recordings.text:
Coordinator: The pilot shows that you accepted all the digital codes that reached your till. Does that mean the scanner worked well?

Till worker: It worked once I had it out. We keep it on the counter when we expect a group. On other days, the cable gets in the way of the people carrying drinks. On Saturday I had to open the drawer, find the scanner and plug it in for one customer. The people behind her thought I was fixing the till.

Coordinator: Did anybody give up while you were doing that?

Till worker: I saw one man leave the line. I don't know whether he had a voucher. Another customer showed his code after the scanner was ready, and the rest of the sale was quick.

Coordinator: Could we move it without affecting the drinks counter?

Till worker: If we put it at the end table, I could finish the current sale before checking a code there. I'd need a clear sign. People would otherwise start to queue at both places.

recordings.title: Two members of the review team
recordings.text:
Mina: I want us to keep the paper cards. People in the morning group collect them for a family member. With email codes, the family member sometimes has to ask for the email to be sent again on the day.

Colin: I agree that choice matters, but we can't give staff two long lists to check at closing. Could both formats show the same reference? A till worker could mark it and we could combine the records at the centre.

Mina: How would they know if the reference had already been used at another café that day?

Colin: A working scanner could tell them whether a digital code was used. A café using the fallback sheet would need to check the reference first. Let's test it with one café that can call us during opening hours.

Mina: So we retain a paper option and try the shared reference in one place. We aren't asking everyone to change how they work at once.

reading.prompt: 1. What do the counts leave out?
options: Attempts that did not result in a meal
Digital codes that were sent
Completed paper transactions
The number of cafés using scanners
reading.explanation: The counts are for recorded uses, not unsuccessful attempts.

reading.prompt: 1. Why did the paper list sometimes take longer to check?
options: A first name appeared more than once.
The scanner was in a drawer.
Staff had to call everyone individually.
The form was missing the café name.
reading.explanation: The manager reported this issue with repeated first names.

reading.prompt: 1. What would the manager need to learn before choosing?
options: Whether the pilot recorded any completed meals
How to make the formats cost the same
How staff and visitors manage each format in less convenient conditions
Which format was first offered at Hill Café
reading.explanation: The final paragraph raises questions about access and simultaneous arrivals.

reading.prompt: 2. Why do different distribution routes matter?
options: The two groups could differ in habits beyond voucher format.
It explains why all users opened email at the café.
Each paper card always went to a different person.
It proves customers choose based on budget.
reading.explanation: How people contact the centre is a possible additional difference.

options: At the start of any normal sale
After an interrupted transaction and after the customer leaves
When the customer picks a format
Only when the main scanner is replaced
reading.explanation: Staff flag an interruption and choose a reason after the guest leaves.

options: An already-used code
A digital code that cannot be displayed
A request for a second meal
A paper list with missing names
reading.explanation: Its purpose is to handle a code that will not load.

listening.prompt: 1. Why was the scanner in a drawer?
options: It had stopped working.
Only the coordinator could use it.
There was nowhere to plug it in.
Its cable got in the way near drinks.
listening.explanation: The worker identifies the route for carrying drinks as the constraint.

listening.prompt: 1. What can we conclude about the man who left?
options: He left after a voucher was rejected.
He had already redeemed his voucher.
His reason and whether he had a voucher are unknown.
His digital code was later accepted.
listening.explanation: The till worker saw him leave but does not know his situation.

listening.prompt: 1. What would staff need at the end table?
options: A sign to prevent confusion about where to queue
A second receipt for every sale
An extra paper voucher on the counter
A way to avoid finishing the sale first
listening.explanation: The sign would help prevent people forming two lines unexpectedly.

listening.prompt: 2. Why keep paper according to Mina?
options: It avoids evening checks.
It can be collected for somebody else.
A paper list can verify digital uses.
All café staff prefer it.
listening.explanation: She describes people collecting cards for family members.

options: A reference may have been used at a different café.
A worker might issue the wrong café name.
A family member could forget where to collect a code.
The centre cannot combine the two lists.
listening.explanation: Mina asks how they would identify prior use elsewhere.

listening.prompt: 2. Which change do they agree to test?
options: All cafés move to paper immediately.
One café tries shared references while retaining paper.
Email codes are removed at the morning session.
Two cafés test picking up new scanners.
listening.explanation: They keep a paper option and limit the shared reference to one café.

grammar.explanation: Although introduces a concession before or after a main claim. Whereas contrasts two facts. While can also set facts beside each other, and can introduce an -ing phrase when both actions belong to the same subject. Avoid adding but after an although clause.

examples.before: Although the scanner worked, but it took time.
examples.after: Although the scanner worked, it took time.
examples.why: Although already connects the concession to its main clause.

examples.before: The list was slow whereas it, codes closed fast.
examples.after: The paper check took longer, whereas the code record was ready at closing.

examples.before: While codes were used. Attempts were not counted.
examples.after: While codes were used, attempts were not counted.
examples.why: Keep the concession joined to the contrasting finding.

questions.prompt: _____ the café logged each meal, its record missed unsuccessful attempts.
options: Despite
Although
During
Because of

questions.prompt: Paper cards arrive in person, _____ digital codes are sent by email.
options: because of
until
afterwards
whereas
Although the reference can be printed, but staff must check it.
Although the reference can be printed, staff must check it.
Despite the reference can be printed, staff must check it.
The reference although can be printed, staff must check it.
questions.explanation: Only the first uses one suitable connector.

questions.prompt: Staff handled the till _____ checking codes.
options: whereas
while
despite of
because of
Because costs were similar, access was equal.
Staff checked access because all results were equal.
Although costs were similar, access still needs checking.
As costs were low, nobody left the queue.
questions.explanation: The concession separates observed cost from an unknown.

questions.prompt: _____ both formats use one reference, the sheets stay separate for now.
options: Despite of
Due to
Although
Yet of
questions.explanation: The opening introduces a full clause.

questions.prompt: The list was quick on Tuesday, _____ Saturday took longer.
options: whereas
instead of
despite
before that

questions.prompt: Which sentence keeps the evidence and its limit distinct?
options: The till accepted the code because nobody left.
The till accepted the code, so everyone was served.
The till accepted the code, although we cannot account for everyone who left.
Although everyone was served, the code was rejected.
questions.explanation: The first keeps the recorded sale and the unknown outcome separate.

grammar.transfer: Make four claims from the sources. Mark two contrasts and two concessions. Check that no concession quietly turns an unknown cause into a known one.

vocabulary.meaning: use a voucher for what it offers
vocabulary.example: Redeem the card at the till.

vocabulary.meaning: an option used when the usual one fails
vocabulary.example: The printed reference is our fallback.

vocabulary.meaning: give someone an official document or code
an exchange that takes place at a till
how many people use an offer
vocabulary.example: The team checked uptake in May.

vocabulary.meaning: stop a process before it finishes
check two sets of records and account for differences
vocabulary.example: Staff reconcile the lists at closing.
The two queues must stay distinct.

vocabulary.meaning: a code used to find a record
vocabulary.example: Please show the reference on the card.
The trial begins at one café.
This card is valid until Friday.

speaking.first: Give a two-minute briefing using one observed interruption, one unknown and one possible fix. Include a line a worker can say to a customer.
speaking.change: The café can contact the centre by phone before noon only.
speaking.second: Redo the briefing with a time limit on the fallback. Say exactly what the worker should offer outside that window.
checklist: Uses one concession and one contrast
States who checks the reference and when.

writing.audience: The centre manager and then people choosing a voucher
writing.first: Draft a 170–200 word recommendation that compares the formats and sets out one measure for people who were not served.
writing.change: Only one café can join the trial, and visitors need a short public notice.
writing.second: Revise the recommendation to fit one site. Add a notice of up to 55 words explaining what to bring if a code does not load.
checklist: Recommendation accounts for the distribution route
The notice contains no promise of a second meal
The measure can distinguish failed and successful attempts.

immersion.goal: Prepare a trial that a café can run during normal service.
constraints: Collect no names for interruption statistics
immersion.change: The only worker able to use the scanner also serves hot drinks at the busiest time.
deliverables: One-page workflow with two exception routes
A tally sheet and an end-of-trial decision rule
checklist: The site and time limits match across artifacts
The procedure explains who checks prior use
The tally covers people who did not reach payment
The trial has a clear change criterion.
